questions.knowledge_point: Rewriting a Triple Integral Defined Over a Cylindrical Solid
questions.problem:
The region $R$ is enclosed inside the cylinder ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=9$ between the surfaces $z=1$ and $z=10-x.$
Express the following triple integral in cylindrical polar coordinates. 

$$
{∭}_{R}z\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}V
$$
questions.worked_solution:
We will use the change of variables formula in the form

$$
{∭}_{R}f(x,y,z)\,dV={∭}_{Δ}\,f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,z)\,r\,dz\,dr\,d\theta .
$$

If $(r,\theta ,z)$ are the cylindrical polar coordinates of a point, then its Cartesian coordinates $(x,y,z)$ can be found by using the formulas

$$
x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,z=z.
$$

First, let's sketch the projection of $R$ onto the $xy$-plane:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14071292/assets/9c4ea0ba92e19a201e3944defa6deb0bc1ee76971adaa809521722b6ac31241f.png)

The region $R$ is a right vertical cylinder of radius $3$ whose axis passes through the point $(0,0)$ in the $xy$-plane, and is

- bounded below by $z=1,$ and

- bounded above by $z=10-x=10-r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .$

As a result, in cylindrical polar coordinates, our region can be expressed as 

$$
Δ={(r,\theta ,z)\,:\,0\le r\le 3,\,0\le \theta <2\pi ,\,1\le z\le 10-r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }.
$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain  

$$
\begin{aligned}{∭}_{R}z\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}V & ={∭}_{Δ}z\sqrt{(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}+(r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2}}\,r\,dz\,dr\,d\theta  \\  & ={∭}_{Δ}z\sqrt{{r}^{2}({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )}\,r\,dz\,dr\,d\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{0}^{3}{\int }_{1}^{10-r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }{r}^{2}z\,dz\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
The region $R$ is enclosed inside the cylinder ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=2$ between the surfaces $z=0$ and $z=\sqrt{16-({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})}.$ Express the following triple integral in cylindrical polar coordinates. 

$$
{∭}_{R}\frac{1}{\sqrt{1+z}}\,\text{d}V
$$
questions.worked_solution:
We will use the change of variables formula in the form

$$
{∭}_{R}f(x,y,z)\,dV={∭}_{Δ}\,f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,z)\,r\,dz\,dr\,d\theta .
$$

If $(r,\theta ,z)$ are the cylindrical polar coordinates of a point, then its Cartesian coordinates $(x,y,z)$ can be found by using the formulas

$$
x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,z=z.
$$

First, let's sketch the projection of $R$ onto the $xy$-plane:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14071292/assets/36839d1fbde65e86df7335d40374fe72a5ff43ed92b89405327406a62dc8763c.png)

The region $R$ is a right vertical cylinder of radius $\sqrt{2}$ whose axis passes through the point $(0,0)$ in the $xy$-plane, and is

- bounded below by $z=0,$ and

- bounded above by $z=\sqrt{16-({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})}=\sqrt{16-{r}^{2}}.$

As a result, in cylindrical polar coordinates, our region can be expressed as 

$$
Δ={(r,\theta ,z)\,:\,0\le r\le \sqrt{2},\,0\le \theta <2\pi ,\,0\le z\le \sqrt{16-{r}^{2}}}.
$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain  

$$
\begin{aligned}{∭}_{R}\frac{1}{\sqrt{z}}\,\text{d}V & ={∭}_{Δ}\frac{1}{\sqrt{1+z}}\cdot r\,dz\,dr\,d\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{2}}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{16-{r}^{2}}}\frac{r}{\sqrt{1+z}}\,dz\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
The region $R$ is enclosed inside the cylinder ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=9$ for $x\le 0,$ between the surfaces $z=x$ and $z={y}^{2}.$ Express the following triple integral in cylindrical polar coordinates. 

$$
{∭}_{R}{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}\,\text{d}V
$$
questions.worked_solution:
We will use the change of variables formula in the form

$$
{∭}_{R}f(x,y,z)\,dV={∭}_{Δ}\,f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,z)\,r\,dz\,dr\,d\theta .
$$

If $(r,\theta ,z)$ are the cylindrical polar coordinates of a point, then its Cartesian coordinates $(x,y,z)$ can be found by using the formulas

$$
x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,z=z.
$$

First, let's sketch the projection of $R$ onto the $xy$-plane:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14071292/assets/16b7c2f69bb20df2faafabf10368776cb69b608bb61eb8432495ae5f146e7100.png)

The region $R$ is one-half of a right vertical cylinder of radius $3$ whose axis passes through the point $(0,0)$ in the $xy$-plane, and is

- bounded below by $z=x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,$ and

- bounded above by $z={y}^{2}={r}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta .$

As a result, in cylindrical polar coordinates, our region can be expressed as 

$$
Δ={(r,\theta ,z)\,:\,0\le r\le 3,\,\frac{\pi }{2}\le \theta <\frac{3\pi }{2},\,r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \le z\le {r}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta }.
$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain  

$$
\begin{aligned}{∭}_{R}{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}\,\text{d}V & ={∭}_{Δ}((r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}-(r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2})\cdot r\,dz\,dr\,d\theta  \\  & ={∭}_{Δ}r({r}^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta -{r}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )\,dz\,dr\,d\theta  \\  & ={∭}_{Δ}{r}^{3}({cos}^{2}⁡\theta -{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )\,dz\,dr\,d\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{3\pi /2}{\int }_{0}^{3}{\int }_{r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }^{{r}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta }{r}^{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta \,dz\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

$$
{∭}_{R}z({x}^{2}-{y}^{2})\,\text{d}V
$$
questions.worked_solution:
We will use the change of variables formula in the form

$$
{∭}_{R}f(x,y,z)\,dV={∭}_{Δ}\,f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,z)\,r\,dz\,dr\,d\theta .
$$

If $(r,\theta ,z)$ are the cylindrical polar coordinates of a point, then its Cartesian coordinates $(x,y,z)$ can be found by using the formulas

$$
x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,z=z.
$$

First, let's sketch the projection of $R$ onto the $xy$-plane:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14071292/assets/7d3ef0b0a9a2f1c9ab60b4ed09f8a0318c57f74236e404baf181e0197ef66002.png)

The region $R$ is one-half of a right vertical cylinder of radius $\sqrt{5}$ whose axis passes through the point $(0,0)$ in the $xy$-plane, and is

- bounded below by $z=-1,$ and

- bounded above by $z=y+2=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +2.$

As a result, in cylindrical polar coordinates, our region can be expressed as 

$$
Δ={(r,\theta ,z)\,:\,0\le r\le \sqrt{5},\,0\le \theta \le \pi ,\,-1\le z\le r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +2}.

$$

$$

questions.knowledge_point: Rewriting a Triple Integral Defined Over a Shifted Cylindrical Solid
questions.problem:
If the solid region $R$ is given by 

$$
R={(x,y,z)\,:\,(x+3)^{2}+{y}^{2}\le 9,\,-8\le z\le x+2},
$$

then ${∭}_{R}\frac{1}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+1}}\,\text{d}V=$
questions.worked_solution:
We will use the change of variables formula in the form

$$
{∭}_{R}f(x,y,z)\,dV={∭}_{Δ}\,f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,z)\,r\,dz\,dr\,d\theta .
$$

If $(r,\theta ,z)$ are the cylindrical polar coordinates of a point, then its Cartesian coordinates $(x,y,z)$ can be found by using the formulas

$$
x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,z=z.
$$

First, let's sketch the projection of $R$ onto the $xy$-plane:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14071292/assets/3c03dde21942c60de527ace896bb51ad8070781126d72f5be5e2f6069700736d.png)

The region $R$ is a right vertical cylinder of radius $3$ whose axis passes through the point $(-3,0)$ in the $xy$-plane, and is

- bounded below by $z=-8,$ and

- bounded above by $z=x+2=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +2.$

With that in mind, let's write the equation $(x+3)^{2}+{y}^{2}=9$ in polar coordinates:

$$
\begin{aligned}(x+3)^{2}+{y}^{2} & =9 \\ {(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +3)}^{2}+{(r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )}^{2} & =9 \\ {r}^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +6r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +9+{r}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta  & =9 \\ {r}^{2}({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )+6r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & =0 \\ {r}^{2}+6r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & =0 \\ r(r+6\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

 

Since $r$ cannot be identical to zero on the entire circle, we must have $r=-6\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .$

As a result, in cylindrical polar coordinates, our region can be expressed as 

$$
Δ={(r,\theta ,z)\,:\,0\le r\le -6\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,\frac{\pi }{2}\le \theta \le \frac{3\pi }{2},\,-8\le z\le r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +2}.
$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain  

$$
\begin{aligned}{∭}_{R}\frac{1}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+1}}\,\text{d}V & ={∭}_{Δ}\frac{1}{\sqrt{(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}+(r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2}+1}}\cdot r\,dz\,dr\,d\theta  \\  & ={∭}_{Δ}\frac{r}{\sqrt{{r}^{2}({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )+1}}\,dz\,dr\,d\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{3\pi /2}{\int }_{0}^{-6\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }{\int }_{-8}^{r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +2}\frac{r}{\sqrt{{r}^{2}+1}}\,dz\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
If the solid region $R$ is given by 

$$
R={(x,y,z)\,:\,(x-3)^{2}+{y}^{2}\le 9,\,y\le 0,\,y\le z\le 6},
$$

then ${∭}_{R}\frac{1}{\sqrt{z+1}}\,\text{d}V=$
questions.worked_solution:
We will use the change of variables formula in the form

$$
{∭}_{R}f(x,y,z)\,dV={∭}_{Δ}\,f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,z)\,r\,dz\,dr\,d\theta .
$$

If $(r,\theta ,z)$ are the cylindrical polar coordinates of a point, then its Cartesian coordinates $(x,y,z)$ can be found by using the formulas

$$
x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,z=z.
$$

First, let's sketch the projection of $R$ onto the $xy$-plane:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14071292/assets/ccc5cab37aed89c0d701ce0195414796211ddc73a498eaaa1ff145a45c42e9fd.png)

The region $R$ is one-half of a right vertical cylinder of radius $3$ whose axis passes through the point $(3,0)$ in the $xy$-plane, and is

- bounded below by $z=y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,$ and

- bounded above by $z=6.$

With that in mind, let's now write the $(x-3)^{2}+{y}^{2}=9$ in polar coordinates:

$$
\begin{aligned}(x-3)^{2}+{y}^{2} & =9 \\ (r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -3)^{2}+(r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2} & =3 \\ {r}^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta -6r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +9+{r}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta  & =9 \\ {r}^{2}({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )-6r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & =0 \\ {r}^{2}-6r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & =0 \\ r(r-6\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

 

Since $r$ cannot be identical to zero on the entire semicircle, we must have $r=6\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .$

As a result, in cylindrical polar coordinates, our region can be expressed as 

$$
Δ={(r,\theta ,z)\,:\,0\le r\le 6\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,\frac{3\pi }{2}\le \theta \le 2\pi ,\,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \le z\le 6}.
$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain  

$$
\begin{aligned}{∭}_{R}\frac{1}{\sqrt{z+1}}\,\text{d}V & ={∭}_{Δ}\frac{1}{\sqrt{z+1}}\cdot r\,dz\,dr\,d\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{3\pi /2}^{2\pi }{\int }_{0}^{6\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }{\int }_{r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }^{6}\frac{r}{\sqrt{z+1}}\,dz\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

mathematical_assessment.explanation: Recomputing gives r²−6r cosθ≤0, so 0≤r≤6 cosθ and 3π/2≤θ≤2π. The height bounds are r sinθ≤z≤6, and the Jacobian contributes r. These formally match option e. The earlier uncertainty remains: R contains (3,−2,−3/2), where √(z+1) is not real. Thus the stated real integral is undefined; option e is its formal transformation only.

questions.problem:
Evaluate the triple integral 

$$
{∭}_{R}\frac{z}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}}\,\text{d}V
$$

over the region $R$ enclosed inside the cylinder ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=9$ and between the surfaces $z=0$ and $z=\sqrt{9-({x}^{2}-{y}^{2})}.$
questions.worked_solution:
We will use the change of variables formula in the form

$$
{∭}_{R}f(x,y,z)\,dV={∭}_{Δ}\,f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,z)\,r\,dz\,dr\,d\theta .
$$

If $(r,\theta ,z)$ are the cylindrical polar coordinates of a point, then its Cartesian coordinates $(x,y,z)$ can be found by using the formulas

$$
x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,z=z.
$$

First, let's sketch the projection of $R$ onto the $xy$-plane:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14071292/assets/9c4ea0ba92e19a201e3944defa6deb0bc1ee76971adaa809521722b6ac31241f.png)

The region $R$ is a right vertical cylinder of radius $3$ whose axis passes through the point $(0,0)$ in the $xy$-plane, and is

- bounded below by $z=0,$ and

- bounded above by $z=\sqrt{9-({x}^{2}-{y}^{2})}=\sqrt{9-{r}^{2}({cos}^{2}⁡\theta -{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )}=\sqrt{9-{r}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta )}.$

As a result, in cylindrical polar coordinates, our region can be expressed as 

$$
Δ={(r,\theta ,z)\,:\,0\le r\le 3,\,0\le \theta <2\pi ,\,0\le z\le \sqrt{9-{r}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta )}}.
$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain  

$$
\begin{aligned}{∭}_{R}\frac{z}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}}\,\text{d}V & ={∭}_{Δ}\frac{z}{\sqrt{{r}^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{r}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }}\,r\,dz\,dr\,d\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{0}^{3}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{9-{r}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta )}}z\,dz\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{0}^{3}{[\frac{1}{2}{z}^{2}]}_{z=0}^{z=\sqrt{9-{r}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta )}}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{0}^{3}\frac{1}{2}{(\sqrt{9-{r}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta )})}^{2}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{0}^{3}\frac{1}{2}(9-{r}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta ))\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{[\frac{9}{2}r-\frac{1}{6}{r}^{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta )]}_{r=0}^{r=3}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\frac{9}{2}(3)-\frac{1}{6}(3)^{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta )\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\frac{27}{2}-\frac{9}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta )\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={[\frac{27}{2}\theta -\frac{9}{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )]}_{\theta =0}^{\theta =2\pi } \\  & =\frac{27}{2}(2\pi -0)-\frac{9}{4}(0-0) \\  & =27\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{∭}_{R}{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}\,\text{d}V & ={∭}_{Δ}({(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )}^{2}+{(r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )}^{2})\,r\,dz\,dr\,d\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{r}^{1}{r}^{3}\,dz\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{0}^{1}{r}^{3}[z]_{z=r}^{z=1}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{0}^{1}{r}^{3}(1-r)\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{0}^{1}{r}^{3}-{r}^{4}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{[\frac{1}{4}{r}^{4}-\frac{1}{5}{r}^{5}]}_{r=0}^{r=1}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\frac{1}{4}-\frac{1}{5}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\frac{1}{20}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={[\frac{1}{20}\theta ]}_{\theta =0}^{\theta =2\pi } \\  & =\frac{1}{20}(2\pi -0) \\  & =\frac{\pi }{10}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Evaluate the triple integral 

$$
{∭}_{R}x\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}V
$$

over the region $R$ enclosed inside the cylinder ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=3$ for $x\ge 0$ and between the surfaces $z=y$ and $z=y+4.$
questions.worked_solution:
We will use the change of variables formula in the form

$$
{∭}_{R}f(x,y,z)\,dV={∭}_{Δ}\,f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,z)\,r\,dz\,dr\,d\theta .
$$

If $(r,\theta ,z)$ are the cylindrical polar coordinates of a point, then its Cartesian coordinates $(x,y,z)$ can be found by using the formulas

$$
x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,z=z.
$$

First, let's sketch the projection of $R$ onto the $xy$-plane:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14071292/assets/e289cfbd210112a619018a7b905f7f2b1a9859ecb84b2517dd745705624d79d7.png)

The region $R$ is a right vertical cylinder of radius $\sqrt{3}$ whose axis passes through the point $(0,0)$ in the $xy$-plane, and is

- bounded below by $z=y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,$ and

- bounded above by $z=y+4=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +4.$

As a result, in cylindrical polar coordinates, our region can be expressed as 

$$
Δ={(r,\theta ,z)\,:\,0\le r\le \sqrt{3},\,-\frac{\pi }{2}\le \theta <\frac{\pi }{2},\,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \le z\le r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +4}.
$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain  

$$
\begin{aligned}{∭}_{R}x\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}V & ={∭}_{Δ}r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \sqrt{(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}+(r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2}}\,r\,dz\,dr\,d\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{3}}{\int }_{r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }^{r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +4}{r}^{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,dz\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{3}}{r}^{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta [z]_{z=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }^{z=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +4}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{3}}{r}^{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta (r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +4-r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{3}}4{r}^{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}[{r}^{4}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ]_{r=0}^{r=\sqrt{3}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}(\sqrt{3})^{4}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}9\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =[9\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ]_{\theta =-\pi /2}^{\theta =\pi /2} \\  & =9(1-(-1)) \\  & =18.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Evaluate the triple integral 

$$
{∭}_{R}2xz\,\text{d}V
$$

over the region $R$ enclosed inside the cylinder ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=1$ for $y\ge 0$ and between the surfaces $z=-x$ and $z=x+2.$
questions.worked_solution:
We will use the change of variables formula in the form

$$
{∭}_{R}f(x,y,z)\,dV={∭}_{Δ}\,f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,z)\,r\,dz\,dr\,d\theta .
$$

If $(r,\theta ,z)$ are the cylindrical polar coordinates of a point, then its Cartesian coordinates $(x,y,z)$ can be found by using the formulas

$$
x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,z=z.
$$

First, let's sketch the projection of $R$ onto the $xy$-plane:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14071292/assets/f837d76caa5a6fd2c2de9a628a77c211fc12be6733fec4f1d3332b9c8ff0991c.png)

The region $R$ is a right vertical cylinder of radius $1$ whose axis passes through the point $(0,0)$ in the $xy$-plane, and is

- bounded below by $z=-x=-r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,$ and

- bounded above by $z=x+2=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +2.$

As a result, in cylindrical polar coordinates, our region can be expressed as 

$$
Δ={(r,\theta ,z)\,:\,0\le r\le 1,\,0\le \theta <\pi ,\,-r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \le z\le r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +2}.
$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain  

$$
\begin{aligned}{∭}_{R}2xz\,\text{d}V & ={∭}_{Δ}2z\cdot r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \cdot r\,dz\,dr\,d\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{-r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }^{r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +2}2z{r}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,dz\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }{\int }_{0}^{1}{r}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta [{z}^{2}]_{z=-r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }^{z=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +2}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }{\int }_{0}^{1}{r}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ({(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +2)}^{2}-{(-r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )}^{2})\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }{\int }_{0}^{1}{r}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ({r}^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +4r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +4-{r}^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta )\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }{\int }_{0}^{1}4{r}^{3}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +4{r}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }[{r}^{4}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +\frac{4}{3}{r}^{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ]_{r=0}^{r=1}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +\frac{4}{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }\frac{1}{2}(1+\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta ))+\frac{4}{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }\frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta )+\frac{4}{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={[\frac{1}{2}\theta +\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )+\frac{4}{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ]}_{\theta =0}^{\theta =\pi } \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\pi -0)+\frac{1}{4}(0-0)+\frac{4}{3}(0-0) \\  & =\frac{\pi }{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Evaluate the triple integral 

$$
{∭}_{R}4\,\text{d}V
$$

over the region $R$ enclosed inside the cylinder ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=2$ for $y\ge 0$ and between the surfaces $z=0$ and $z=6-2x.$
questions.worked_solution:
We will use the change of variables formula in the form

$$
{∭}_{R}f(x,y,z)\,dV={∭}_{Δ}\,f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,z)\,r\,dz\,dr\,d\theta .
$$

If $(r,\theta ,z)$ are the cylindrical polar coordinates of a point, then its Cartesian coordinates $(x,y,z)$ can be found by using the formulas

$$
x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,z=z.
$$

First, let's sketch the projection of $R$ onto the $xy$-plane:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14071292/assets/6fe710e758ccda9a826d79f8219dc82b25f8cc39f65d92f02a6c28594c428a96.png)

The region $R$ is a right vertical cylinder of radius $\sqrt{2}$ whose axis passes through the point $(0,0)$ in the $xy$-plane, and is

- bounded below by $z=0,$ and

- bounded above by $z=6-2x=6-2r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .$

As a result, in cylindrical polar coordinates, our region can be expressed as 

$$
Δ={(r,\theta ,z)\,:\,0\le r\le \sqrt{2},\,0\le \theta <\pi ,\,0\le z\le 6-2r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }.
$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain  

$$
\begin{aligned}{∭}_{R}4\,\text{d}V & ={∭}_{Δ}4\,r\,dz\,dr\,d\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{2}}{\int }_{0}^{6-2r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }4r\,dz\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{2}}4r[z]_{z=0}^{z=6-2r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{2}}4r(6-2r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{2}}24r-8{r}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }{[12{r}^{2}-\frac{8}{3}{r}^{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ]}_{r=0}^{r=\sqrt{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }12(\sqrt{2})^{2}-\frac{8}{3}(\sqrt{2})^{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }24-\frac{16\sqrt{2}}{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={[24\theta -\frac{16\sqrt{2}}{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ]}_{\theta =0}^{\theta =\pi } \\  & =24(\pi -0)-\frac{16\sqrt{2}}{3}(0-0) \\  & =24\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.problem:
The region $R$ is enclosed inside the cylinder $x^2 + y^2 = 4$ for $y \geq 0$ between the surfaces $z =0$ and $z = 10 - x.$ Express the following triple integral in cylindrical polar coordinates. 

$$
\displaystyle \iiint\limits_R y \:\textrm{d}V
$$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
We will use the change of variables formula in the form

$$
\iiint\limits_{R} f(x,y,z) \, \mathrm{d}V = 
\iiint\limits_{\Delta} \, f(r \cos\theta, r\sin\theta, z) \:  r \: \mathrm{d}z \, \mathrm{d}r \, \mathrm{d}\theta.
$$

If $(r, \theta, z)$ are the cylindrical polar coordinates of a point, then its Cartesian coordinates $(x,y,z)$ can be found by using the formulas

$$
x = r\cos\theta, \qquad
y = r\sin\theta, \qquad 
z = z.
$$

First, let's sketch the projection of $R$ onto the $xy$-plane:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14071292/assets/9ad0d507a5440cfce9595e9054457fd733ae412d9a57b0a85238b4773ff0a0c7.png)

The region $R$ is one-half of a right vertical cylinder of radius $2$ whose axis passes through the point $(0,0)$ in the $xy$-plane, and is

- bounded below by $z=0,$ and

- bounded above by $z=10-x = 10 - r\cos\theta.$

As a result, in cylindrical polar coordinates, our region can be expressed as 

$$
\Delta = \left\{ (r,\theta,z) \, : \, 0 \leq r \leq 2, \: 0 \leq \theta \leq \pi, \: 0 \leq z \leq 10-r\cos\theta \right\}.
$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain  

$$
\begin{aligned}{∭}_{R}y\,\text{d}V & ={∭}_{Δ}(r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\cdot r\,dz\,dr\,d\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }{\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{10-r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }{r}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,dz\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.problem:
If the solid region $R$ is given by 

$$
R = \left\{ (x,y,z) \, : \, (x-1)^2 + y^2 \leq 1, \: -2 \leq z \leq 4-y \right\},
$$

then express the triple integral

$$
\displaystyle \iiint\limits_R \sqrt{x^2 + y^2} \: \textrm{d}V
$$

as an equivalent integral in cylindrical polar coordinates.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
We will use the change of variables formula in the form

$$
\iiint\limits_{R} f(x,y,z) \, \mathrm{d}V = 
\iiint\limits_{\Delta} \, f(r \cos\theta, r\sin\theta, z) \:  r \: \mathrm{d}z \, \mathrm{d}r \, \mathrm{d}\theta.
$$

If $(r, \theta, z)$ are the cylindrical polar coordinates of a point, then its Cartesian coordinates $(x,y,z)$ can be found by using the formulas

$$
x = r\cos\theta, \qquad
y = r\sin\theta, \qquad 
z = z.
$$

First, let's sketch the projection of $R$ onto the $xy$-plane:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14071292/assets/a551e379767395a2422f690a66fc38defab64cff03c752c0c9a5a0748561d2f7.png)

The region $R$ is a right vertical cylinder of radius $1$ whose axis passes through the point $(1,0)$ in the $xy$-plane, and is

- bounded below by $z = -2,$ and

- bounded above by $z = 4 - y = 4 - r\sin{\theta}.$

With that in mind, let's write the equation $(x-1)^2 + y^2 = 1$ in polar coordinates:

$$
\begin{aligned}(x-1)^{2}+{y}^{2} & =1 \\ {(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -1)}^{2}+{(r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )}^{2} & =1 \\ {r}^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta -2r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +1+{r}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta  & =1 \\ {r}^{2}({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )-2r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & =0 \\ {r}^{2}-2r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & =0 \\ r(r-2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

 

Since $r$ cannot be identical to zero on the entire circle, we must have $r = 2\cos{\theta}.$

As a result, in cylindrical polar coordinates, our region can be expressed as 

$$
\Delta = \left\{ (r,\theta,z) \, : \, 0 \leq r \leq 2\cos{\theta}, \: -\dfrac{\pi}{2} \leq \theta \leq \dfrac{\pi}{2}, \: -2 \leq z \leq 4-r\sin{\theta} \right\}.
$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain  

$$
\begin{aligned}{∭}_{R}\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}V & ={∭}_{Δ}\sqrt{(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}+(r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2}}\,r\,dz\,dr\,d\theta  \\  & ={∭}_{Δ}\sqrt{{r}^{2}({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )}\,r\,dz\,dr\,d\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}{\int }_{0}^{2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }{\int }_{-2}^{4-r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }{r}^{2}\,dz\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.problem:
Evaluate the triple integral 

$$
\displaystyle \iiint\limits_R x+2y \:\textrm{d}V
$$

over the region $R$ enclosed inside the cylinder $x^2+y^2=5$ for $x\geq 0,$ $y\geq 0$ and between the surfaces $z=y$ and $z=y+3.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
We will use the change of variables formula in the form

$$
\iiint\limits_{R} f(x,y,z) \, \mathrm{d}V = 
\iiint\limits_{\Delta} \, f(r \cos\theta, r\sin\theta, z) \:  r \: \mathrm{d}z \, \mathrm{d}r \, \mathrm{d}\theta.
$$

If $(r, \theta, z)$ are the cylindrical polar coordinates of a point, then its Cartesian coordinates $(x,y,z)$ can be found by using the formulas

$$
x = r\cos\theta, \qquad
y = r\sin\theta, \qquad 
z = z.
$$

First, let's sketch the projection of $R$ onto the $xy$-plane:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14071292/assets/b7b37ffe8e97ed4a661ee98750894641c6ed3354864dd5b54d2ed076e4fdb69b.png)

The region $R$ is a right vertical cylinder of radius $\sqrt{5}$ whose axis passes through the point $(0,0)$ in the $xy$-plane, and is

- bounded below by $z=y=r\sin\theta,$ and

- bounded above by $z=y+3=r\sin\theta + 3.$

As a result, in cylindrical polar coordinates, our region can be expressed as 

$$
\Delta = \left\{ (r,\theta,z) \, : \, 0 \leq r \leq \sqrt{5}, \: 0 \leq \theta \lt \dfrac{\pi}{2}, \: r\sin\theta \leq z \leq r\sin\theta + 3\right\}.
$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain  

$$
\begin{aligned}{∭}_{R}x+2y\,\text{d}V & ={∭}_{Δ}(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +2r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\,dz\,dr\,d\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{5}}{\int }_{r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }^{r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +3}{r}^{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,dz\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{5}}{r}^{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )[z]_{z=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }^{z=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +3}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{5}}{r}^{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )(r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +3-r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{5}}3{r}^{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}[{r}^{3}(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )]_{r=0}^{r=\sqrt{5}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{(\sqrt{5})}^{3}(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}5\sqrt{5}(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =5\sqrt{5}[\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta -2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ]_{\theta =0}^{\theta =\pi /2} \\  & =5\sqrt{5}(1-0)-10\sqrt{5}(0-1) \\  & =15\sqrt{5}.\end{aligned}
$$
